title: A triangle drawn on the Earth
hook: You learned a triangle's angles add to 180°. Draw one big enough on a globe and measure.

knows: that a flat triangle's angles add to 180°
the equator, the North Pole and lines of longitude
doesNotKnow: that the 180° rule holds only on a flat plane
that on a sphere the extra angle measures the triangle's area

misconception: Every triangle has angles summing to 180 degrees.
objective: The learner can explain that a triangle on a sphere has angles adding to more than 180°, that the pole-equator triangle to 90°E has three right angles (270°), and that the excess in radians times R² is its area.

claims.text: The triangle from the North Pole to 0°,0° to 90°E on the equator has three right angles, so its angles add to 270°.
claims.source: Meridians meet the equator at right angles; the meridians 0° and 90°E meet at the pole at 90°. Demo.tsx computes each corner angle from 3-D tangent vectors (cornerAngle) on the same corners it draws: 90°, 90°, 90° at 90°E. Builder re-ran in node (scratch c.mjs): sum 270.000. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Node: cornerAngle at 90E gives 90, 90, 90 (sum 270.000); meridians meet the equator at right angles.

claims.text: On a sphere a triangle's angles add to 180° plus the excess, and the excess measures the area: each degree over 180° is 1/720 of the sphere's surface (Girard's theorem: area = excess in radians × R², and the whole sphere, 4πR², corresponds to 720°).
claims.source: Girard's theorem (Albert Girard, 1629); any spherical trigonometry text, e.g. Todhunter, Spherical Trigonometry (1886), ch. on area. From memory, not checked online. The stage shows both numbers side by side: geoArea x R² and (sum - 180°) in radians x R² agree at every slider stop 15°-135°E (scratch c.mjs). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Girard's theorem: spherical excess (radians) x R^2 = area. Node: at 15,30,60,90,135E geoArea x R^2 = (sum-180) rad x R^2 to 3 d.p. (10.626, 21.253, 42.505, 63.758, 95.637 M km2). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 19): Derivation (lune argument): the three pairs of lunes have area 4R^2(A+B+C) and cover the sphere once plus the triangle and its antipode three extra times, so 4R^2(A+B+C) = 4 pi R^2 + 4T, T = R^2(A+B+C-pi). For the stage's pole-equator triangle (90, 90, lambda) this is lambda R^2: node 10.626, 21.253, 42.505, 63.758, 95.637 M km2 at 15, 30, 60, 90, 135E, matching pass 4's geoArea values. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own derivation (lune argument): 4R^2(A+B+C) = 4 pi R^2 + 4T, so T = R^2 (A+B+C-pi); one degree of excess is (pi/180) R^2 / (4 pi R^2) = 1/720 of the sphere. Own node with the stage's cornerAngle and d3-geo geoArea (fc22-5/tri.mjs): geoArea x R^2 equals excess x R^2 to 3 d.p. at 30-150E. Todhunter not opened; not needed for the sentence.

claims.text: With the corner at 90°E the triangle covers about 63.8 million km², one-eighth (12.5%) of the Earth's 510 million km² surface.
claims.source: Sphere of radius R = 6,371.0088 km (EARTH_RADIUS_KM): (π/2) R² = 63.758 million km²; 4πR² = 510.066 million km². d3-geo geoArea on the exact corners gives 63.758 (scratch c.mjs). The Earth is modelled as a sphere. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Node: (pi/2) R^2 = 63.758 M km2 with R = 6371.0088; 4 pi R^2 = 510.066 M km2; ratio exactly 1/8 = 12.5%. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node: R = 6,371.0088 km; (pi/2) R^2 = 63.758 M km2 (geoArea agrees); 4 pi R^2 = 510.066 M km2; ratio 1/8 = 12.5%. Reveal text: '63.8 M km², one-eighth of the Earth's 510 M km²'. Spherical model disclosed.

claims.text: The 180° rule holds only on a flat surface; on a sphere the sides bulge outward and the angles add up to more.
claims.source: Follows from c2: excess = area / R² > 0 for any triangle of positive area on a sphere; it tends to 0 as the triangle shrinks relative to R. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Follows from Girard (excess = area/R^2 > 0). 'Holds only on a flat surface' is read as zero-curvature geometry; on negatively curved surfaces the sum is less than 180, which the lesson does not discuss. 'Bulge outward' is a picture of how great-circle sides look on a globe view. Non-blocking.

claims.text: Tiny triangles have almost no excess, which is why a triangle on paper shows 180°.
claims.source: Excess = area / R². A 1 km² triangle on the Earth has excess 1 / 6,371² rad, about 0.0000014°. The stage's smallest triangle (15°E) has 15° of excess; the claim is an extrapolation stated in the reveal. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Node: a 1 km2 triangle has excess 1/R^2 rad = 0.0000014 deg; stage's smallest triangle (15E) has 15 deg, so the claim is an extrapolation from the formula, stated as such.

claims.text: On the stage, with corners at the North Pole, 0°,0° and a third corner on the equator: at 30°E the angles add to 210° and the triangle is 4.2% of Earth; at 60°E, 240° and 8.3%; at 90°E, 270° and 12.5%; at 120°E, 300° and 16.7%; at 150°E, 330° and 20.8%.
claims.source: The two equator corners are right angles (meridians meet the equator at 90°) and the pole angle equals the longitude L, so the sum is 180° + L and the share of Earth is L/720 (claim c2): 30/720 = 4.17%, 60/720 = 8.33%, 90/720 = 12.5%, 120/720 = 16.67%, 150/720 = 20.83%. The stage computes the same from triangle() in Demo.tsx (cornerAngle and d3 geoArea). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node with the stage's triangle(): sums 210, 240, 270, 300, 330 degrees; shares 4.2%, 8.3%, 12.5%, 16.7%, 20.8% via pct() (toFixed(1)); equals (L/720) x 100. Slider runs 30-150 in steps of 30.

recall.question: A triangle drawn on a globe covers a quarter of one hemisphere. What can you say about its angles?
recall.why: On a sphere the sides bulge outward; the angle sum exceeds 180° by an amount proportional to the triangle's area.
